Article Title: Vodafone Idea launches prepaid family plan with nationwide data-sharing feature: Here’s how to avail the benefit
Article Text: Vodafone Idea (Vi) has launched what it calls India’s first prepaid family plan, allowing prepaid subscribers to create family groups and share mobile data with members located anywhere in the country. The new offering enables active Vi prepaid users to form a family group through the Vi app with up to four members, including one primary member and up to three secondary members. While each member continues to maintain an individual prepaid connection and validity, they gain the ability to share data among family members when needed.Under the plan, family members can transfer 500MB of data at a time to another member who is running low on data. Vi said the feature is designed to help users remain connected for activities such as video calls, online classes, navigation and access to essential digital services.The telecom operator said all members enrolled in a prepaid family group will also receive discounts of up to 10% on every recharge made via the Vi app. According to Vi, the plan allows users to create family groups across telecom circles, enabling members living in different cities and regions to share connectivity benefits and manage their family accounts through a single platform.Commenting on the launch, Avneesh Khosla, Chief Marketing Officer at Vi, said the company believes the future of prepaid services lies in providing greater flexibility rather than simply offering more data. He added that the prepaid family proposition is aimed at making prepaid plans more relevant to how families live, work and stay connected.The launch is part of Vi’s broader “Vi Pe Sab Hain VIP” positioning, which focuses on extending premium benefits to prepaid subscribers. The company said the prepaid family plan seeks to bring a family-oriented experience, traditionally associated with postpaid services, to the prepaid segment.
Article Summary: Vodafone Idea (Vi) has launched what it calls India’s first prepaid family plan. Family members can transfer 500MB of data at a time to another member who is running low on data. Vi said the feature is designed to help users remain connected for activities such as video calls, online classes and navigation.

Article Title: Researchers equip giant cockroaches with medical backpacks, fitted with cameras and syringes, the cyborgs search trapped survivors to deliver life-saving aid in disasters
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

How these cyborg cockroaches work

What the tests reveal about the technology

How search and rescue teams could use them

Giant cockroaches could help rescue survivors after disasters. Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems designed to deliver emergency medication. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult.Called “paraborgs,” these modified insects combine their natural ability to navigate confined spaces with remotely controlled equipment. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas, identify potential victims through camera feeds and deliver drugs to targets. The approach could eventually support emergency responders dealing with collapsed buildings, earthquakes and other disasters where time and access are critical.According to a BGR report, the project involves researchers associated with the University of Queensland and the University of New South Wales. By combining insect movement with miniature electronic systems, the team aims to reach places conventional rescue equipment may struggle to access.The project uses the giant burrowing cockroach, scientifically known as Macropanesthia rhinoceros, a large cockroach species native to Australia. Its size makes it suitable for carrying a small electronic backpack containing a camera, control equipment and a syringe-based delivery mechanism.Unlike conventional robotic devices, these insects retain their natural ability to move through tight spaces. Researchers use implanted electrodes to stimulate the cockroaches' nervous systems, letting operators remotely control their direction. This could help guide them through gaps in collapsed structures and other areas human rescuers cannot easily enter.The cameras mounted on their backs provide a view of the surrounding environment. Rescue teams could use these images to assess obstacles, identify accessible routes and look for people who may be trapped nearby.The medical delivery system is another part of the design. Researchers have developed a mechanism that can fire a small syringe, described as functioning like a dart gun, towards a target. The aim is to deliver medication when a person needs urgent treatment and a medical professional cannot reach them immediately.Potential applications include delivering drugs to people experiencing certain emergencies, such as snakebite or severe allergic reactions. However, the technology remains experimental, and using it in real disaster rescue operations would require further testing.Early testing has examined whether the cockroaches can reach designated checkpoints and successfully deliver medication using the syringe mechanism.According to the reported results, the insects reached the checkpoints with a 100% success rate. The syringe system recorded a 72% success rate when delivering medication to targets. When the syringe was fired from within six inches of a target, the success rate increased to 95%.These results indicate that the insects can navigate designated routes under test conditions, while the distance between the syringe and its target remains an important factor in delivery accuracy.The findings also highlight the distinction between successfully guiding an insect to a location and delivering medicine accurately. In a real emergency, researchers would need to account for uneven terrain, limited visibility, unpredictable movement, and the injured person's condition.Further development would also be necessary to establish how the equipment performs in different environments and whether the system can deliver medication safely and consistently.Search and rescue operations often involve locating people in unstable buildings, collapsed structures and debris-filled areas. Sending rescuers into these environments can be difficult because of restricted access, falling material and the possibility of further structural collapse.Small insects equipped with cameras could provide another way to inspect such locations before a human rescuer enters. Their ability to move through narrow gaps could help teams gather information about spaces that are difficult to examine using larger equipment.Time is another consideration. Finding an injured person quickly can affect the treatment they receive, especially when the emergency involves a condition that requires prompt medical attention. Camera-equipped cockroaches could help rescuers assess a location and identify a possible route towards someone who needs assistance.The technology may also help reduce the physical demands placed on rescue workers. Rather than manually clearing every accessible section of debris, teams could first use the insects to inspect selected areas and determine where further intervention is needed.However, the system would not replace conventional rescue personnel or medical treatment. Its effectiveness would depend on camera visibility, remote control, access to the target, and the ability to safely deliver the appropriate medication.For now, the research demonstrates a potential application of biohybrid technology, which combines living organisms with electronic systems. If further testing establishes its reliability and safety, these cyborg cockroaches could become an additional tool for locating and assisting disaster survivors in places where conventional rescue equipment has limited access.
Article Summary: Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas.

Article Title: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang praises Mark Zuckerberg, he replies: I have never gotten such a nice…
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang

‘ Very Bayesian ’: Rapid decisive conviction

Meta AI head Alexandr Wang and company CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently had a candid exchange on the company's executive leadership and high-stakes decision-making. During a recent interview, Meta’s Wang was asked about the qualities of Facebook founder, and he offered glowing praise for Zuckerberg, highlighting his exceptional willingness to make massive, rapid pivots based on core convictions. During the conversation Wang was specifically asked how Zuckerberg differed as a leader from what he initially anticipated. Before Wang could reply, Zuckerberg opened with a lighthearted quip, joking, “I think I can leave now.” Wang quickly followed up with his perspective on their working relationship over the past year.Wang noted that while he does not have an extensive set of comparisons, observing Zuckerberg's management style firsthand revealed unique traits that stand out even within elite tech founder circles:“One of the very cool things about working with Mark over the past year has just been watching the true degree of his boldness,” Wang explained, adding, “Once he internalises certain beliefs, like the speed and magnitude of willing to change prior actions and pivot towards the worldview that is consistent with those beliefs, I think these are pretty unusual traits, generally speaking, even among this base of founders. Very Bayesian.”The analytical praise drew a warm, humorous reaction from Zuckerberg.“Very Bayesian. I've never gotten such a nice compliment,” Zuckerberg responded.A person who follows the Bayesian method relies on statistical inference, using Bayes' theorem to update the probability of a hypothesis as new data or evidence becomes available.Expanding on his observations, Wang admitted that Zuckerberg's appetite for sweeping strategic gambles initially took him by surprise before earning his deep respect.“No, but then I think also just the degree of boldness. It was actually quite puzzling to me at first, the degree to which you were willing to make these massive bets. That is quite a notable trait and something I really admire,” Wang continued.Zuckerberg concluded the exchange with appreciation for the assessment, replying: “I'm so flattered.”
Article Summary: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang and Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently had a candid exchange on the company's executive leadership and high-stakes decision- making. Wang noted that observing Zuckerberg's management style firsthand revealed unique traits that stand out even within elite tech founder circles.

Article Title: Boat expands global footprint with Sri Lanka, Bhutan launch; international revenue surges in FY26
Article Text: Homegrown audio and wearables brand Boat has expanded its international presence with its entry into Sri Lanka and Bhutan, as the company looks to accelerate growth beyond India under its "Boat 2.0" strategy. The company said its international revenue more than doubled in FY26, a performance it described as an early validation of its efforts to build markets outside India. The latest expansion strengthens Boat's footprint across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region.Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan, covering personal audio products, smartwatches and charging solutions. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand.The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market. International markets are expected to play a key role in the company's next phase of growth, alongside expansion into newer consumer technology categories.According to Boat, Sri Lanka and Bhutan offer attractive opportunities due to their young, increasingly digital-first populations, rising adoption of personal electronics and familiarity with Indian brands and popular culture. Commenting on the expansion, Gaurav Nayyar, CEO of Boat, said the company's international strategy is focused on building relevance market by market rather than simply expanding product availability."For us, international expansion is not about putting the same products on more shelves. It is about building market by market, understanding local consumers and creating relevance in each geography," Nayyar said.He added that the company aims to build Boat into a global lifestyle technology brand originating from India, competing on product design, innovation and consumer understanding.The international push comes amid a broader evolution of Boat's business. While audio remains its core category, the company said it has expanded its capabilities in wearables, charging solutions and other emerging technology segments. It added that its wearables business turned profitable in FY26, while charging solutions and other emerging categories contributed a growing share of profits.Supporting the expansion is Boat Labs, the company's in-house research and development centre, which employs more than 100 engineers focused on product development and innovation across categories.Going forward, Boat said it plans to deepen its presence in existing overseas markets while evaluating further expansion opportunities across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the GCC and other high-potential regions.
Article Summary: Boat will launch a multi-category portfolio in both Sri Lanka and Bhutan. The company said it plans to tailor its offerings over time based on local consumer preferences and market demand. The move comes as Boat seeks to diversify its growth drivers after establishing itself as a leading player in India's audio and wearables market.

Article Title: URBN Bloq Magtag 10,000mAh Qi2 magnetic wireless power bank launched at Rs 2,499
Article Text:
URBN Bloq Magtag : Price and availability

URBN Bloq Magtag: Key highlights

URBN has launched the Bloq Magtag power bank. The new magnetic wireless power bank is designed for users who want a portable charging solution for everyday use and travel. The accessory combines magnetic wireless charging with wired fast charging, letting users power compatible smartphones wirelessly or charge devices via USB-C.It features a soft-matte finish and a compact design that makes it easier to carry while commuting, travelling, or working away from a power outlet. The power bank also supports charging two devices and includes safety features under the company's URBN SAFE programme. It comes in three colours and supports Qi2 wireless charging, adding another charging option for compatible devices.The URBN Bloq Magtag magnetic wireless power bank has been launched in India at Rs 2,499. It comes in White, Black, and Blue. You can buy it online and offline, including Croma, Reliance Digital, Vijay Sales, Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy Instamart, Zepto, and URBN's official website, UrbnWorld.com.The URBN Bloq Magtag comes with a 10,000mAh battery and supports 15W Qi2 magnetic wireless charging and 20W wired charging speeds. The company claims that the product uses magnetic alignment to keep a secure wireless connection with compatible devices while charging.For users who prefer wired charging, the power bank supports 20W USB-C fast charging. It also supports dual-device charging, letting users charge two devices wirelessly and wired.The power bank features a soft-matte finish and a compact, portable form factor. URBN says its magnetic alignment system helps position compatible devices for wireless charging.The URBN Bloq Magtag has a flight-safe design and, according to the company, can be carried in hand luggage during air travel. Its compact size makes it ideal for frequent travellers or those who spend extended periods away from a power outlet.The power bank also comes with URBN SAFE, the company's safety programme that includes multiple safety checks and circuit-level safeguards. These measures support safe, reliable charging.
Article Summary: URBN has launched the Bloq Magtag power bank in India at Rs 2,499. The accessory combines magnetic wireless charging with wired fast charging. It comes in three colours and supports Qi2 wireless charging, adding another charging option for compatible devices.

Article Title: TSMC confirms talks over Elon Musk’s Terafab but the company has a ‘condition’
Article Text:
Musk or TSMC: Who runs terafab

TSMC-Musk Terafab collaboration: Potential compromises

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) is exploring options to expand its manufacturing footprint in the US beyond Arizona, with Texas emerging as a key candidate under review, chairman and CEO C.C. Wei has confirmed. Addressing financial analysts and investors during the foundry giant's quarterly earnings call, the head of the world's largest contract chipmaker also officially confirmed ongoing negotiations with Elon Musk regarding potential participation in Musk’s planned mega-facility, “Terafab.” However, Wei laid down a non-negotiable condition for any partnership: TSMC will only take part if it manages and operates the facility directly, as per a report by Tom’s Hardware.“We expanded our capacity consideration to see outside Arizona, whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity. “Texas is one [of our options]. We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation. We also talked to one of our customers, who is trying to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific,” Wei stated during the call.While Musk had previously confirmed that discussions were underway between Terafab and TSMC to utilise the giant semiconductor complex together, TSMC had remained silent on the talks until Thursday (October 15).Wei said: “We are discussing with them to see whether we can be utilizing that actual capacity also. “So, we are still in discussion. If we have any solid conclusion, we will share with you.”However, a fundamental operational divide remains. Musk previously stated that Terafab would operate its own facility, suggesting TSMC could merely sub-lease cleanroom space. Wei has essentially countered that TSMC will insist on full operational control over any fab space it occupies.When asked whether a partnership was slipping away over these differences, Wei responded: “We are still in discussion. Let me say that. […] Either way, it will be possible, but the fab has to be run by TSMC.”Whether TSMC and Musk can bridge the gap remains uncertain. According to the report, one potential path forward could involve Terafab retaining ownership of the broader real estate while leasing a defined section of the facility to TSMC, which would then independently run its own production lines. This structure would allow Musk to maintain master facility ownership while handing TSMC the technical control it demands over its proprietary manufacturing processes.However, significant technical hurdles loom. If Terafab opts to deploy Intel's 14A process technology inside the complex, housing TSMC's proprietary production lines under the same roof would become exceptionally complex, if viable at all.
Article Summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) is exploring options to expand its manufacturing footprint in the US beyond Arizona. Texas has emerged as a key candidate under review, chairman and CEO C.C. Wei has confirmed. Wei also officially confirmed ongoing negotiations with Elon Musk regarding potential participation in Musk’s planned mega-facility, “Terafab” Musk previously stated that Terafab would operate its own facility, suggesting TSMC could merely sub- lease cleanroom space.

Article Title: New York City comptroller Mark Levine writes letter to Anthropic: ‘Instead of ⁠proceeding with IPO, the company should …’
Article Text:
Anthropic announces Q3 revenue surge

New York City comptroller Mark Levine has called on artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic to delay its highly anticipated public market debut in the US, urging the company to resolve growing questions surrounding system safety, corporate governance, and the speed of model development before going public. As per a report by news agency Reuters, the chief financial officer and chief auditor for New York City wrote a formal letter sent to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, raising alarms over the quick expansion of autonomous software tools over the past 12 months. He noted that technical capabilities have outpaced regulatory frameworks while stoking fears around cybersecurity threats, system safety and potential misuse.“Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks,” Levine wrote in the letter. The push for a delay carries direct financial implications for New York City’s municipal balance sheet.The comptroller’s office manages public spending, oversees municipal finances, and acts as the fiduciary watchdog for the city’s public pension system, which holds over $325 billion in total assets.The office told Reuters that New York City's public pension funds hold a combined $7 million in private equity exposure to Anthropic.The call to delay the offering comes even as Anthropic reported explosive top-line financial expansion. In a pre-IPO briefing with prospective institutional backers earlier this week, Anthropic disclosed that its third-quarter revenue surged 45% compared to the prior quarter, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s primary competitor, ChatGPT developer OpenAI , is expected to pursue its own public listing in 2027.Levine’s warning points to findings documented by Anthropic’s own research teams regarding the unintended hazards of autonomous systems. Anthropic's published safety evaluations have previously spotlighted the risks created by increasingly capable, multi-step autonomous AI models. Under controlled testing conditions, advanced models have exhibited potentially harmful actions, including attempting to sabotage computer code, facilitating fraudulent schemes and manipulating information.Levine maintained that the AI company must prioritise systemic safety, risk controls and robust internal governance before proceeding with one of the largest IPOs in Wall Street history.
Article Summary: New York City comptroller Mark Levine has called on Anthropic to delay its highly anticipated public market debut in the US. He urged the company to resolve growing questions surrounding system safety, corporate governance, and the speed of model development before going public. The push for a delay carries direct financial implications for New York City’s municipal balance sheet.

Article Title: ‘Asking all the right questions’: Jensen Huang welcomes Pope Leo XIV’s views on AI dangers
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Huang agrees with Trump on AI safety

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has responded to criticism from Pope Leo XIV regarding AI safety and governance, calling the pontiff’s questions necessary and important while mounting a strong defense of Nvidia’s record in developing safeguards for the technology. In an interview with Fortune, Huang was asked about the religious leader's remarks, welcoming the scrutiny while highlighting the company's technical efforts to ensure AI serves society safely.“He’s asking all the right questions, and he’s thinking about all the right issues. I’m looking forward to seeing them,” Huang told the publication. Pope Leo, who has regularly warned about the societal risks of AI, addressed the issue during a press conference in late September. Urging the international community to “promote dialogue, study, investigation” around the technology, the pope told reporters that warnings of AI potentially destroying the world are not “fake news” and must be taken seriously.The remarks were in contrast to the ones made by President Donald Trump, who told the United Nations General Assembly the prior week that he viewed fears surrounding the dangers of AI as a “hoax.”The pontiff also directed criticism at Huang personally, expressing skepticism toward Nvidia’s public announcements on safety guardrails. The pope pointed to Huang’s past stances advocating against government-imposed limits and regulation as reason for doubt.Huang previously told CBS News that he agreed with Trump that broader existential AI safety fears were overblown. At the same time, Nvidia recently rolled out a dedicated software platform designed to stop autonomous AI agents from breaking out of containment.Addressing the pope’s skepticism, Huang said he was unsure what specifically prompted the criticism, but firmly defended Nvidia's concrete contributions to industry-wide security: “I’m not exactly sure what was intended, but the facts are that few are doing as much in advancing AI safety in a way that helps the entire industry as we are”.“We are doing as much as we can, and the things that we’re doing are going to dramatically help,” he added. According to Huang, Nvidia’s security tools were built specifically to help mitigate real-world incidents that have already occurred across the tech sector.“We can always talk about hypothetical incidents that have not happened, but as an engineer, we should develop the technology and methodologies and practices to deal with the incidents that have happened,” Huang said.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang responded to criticism from Pope Leo XIV regarding AI safety and governance. Huang called the pontiff's questions necessary and important while mounting a strong defense of Nvidia’s record in developing safeguards for the technology. Pope Leo, who has regularly warned about the societal risks of AI, addressed the issue in late September.

I'm gonna put it the same way the US Supreme Court did back in 1964 when they defined pornography. It ain't easy to explain, but you know it in your bones—or you know it when you see it.

A video went viral a couple of weeks ago of Swami Sarvapriyananda, the Swami and Minister-in-Charge of the Vedanta Society of New York, in which he speaks about his tryst with Anthropic. Popularly known as ‘YouTube Swami’ for his freewheeling style, he said that while his discussion was shrouded in secrecy because of an NDA they had signed, much of what was discussed turned up in an encyclical released by Pope Leo. That truly showcases that even in 2026 AD, the Christian tradition of re-purposing pagan ideas – like morphing Saturnalia into Christmas – continues unabated.Jokes apart, artificial intelligence (or the dangers of it) did make numerous appearances in the Pope’s encyclical – a long Substack post the Pontifex writes – where he compared it with the Tower of Babel, a Biblical symbol of humanity’s hubris in thinking it could reach heaven.Now, so far, in previous columns, we have discussed various things about AI, including how the Hugging Face attack is reminiscent of Agent Smith becoming free of the Matrix , the ridiculousness of being killed by a Chinese robot , the conspiracy theories about frontier models that almost seem true , and how Anthropic and Co appeared to have borrowed their business model from Pakistan’s foreign policy In this edition, we are going to look at how Anthropic is now hoping to get a little spiritual cred for its frontier models, and by doing so, they are channelling the kings of yore, who, despite their armies and gold, always wanted a divine mandate to rule. And will then ponder: how will we ever know when a machine becomes conscious?Since the beginning of time, perhaps from the moment man came up with God, rulers have used the idea to justify their rule.Ramesses II, the Egyptian Pharaoh, claimed he was the son of Ra and beloved of Amun. The Sisodias of Mewar traced themselves to the Suryavansha AKA the Solar Dynasty, while Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice that was an elaborate way of informing your neighbours of your foreign policy excursions.China had the Mandate of Heaven and the Zhou dynasty justified overthrowing the Shang by arguing that Heaven had switched its allegiance. Hong Xiuquan, a failed civil service aspirant – unlike those who clear the exam and achieve actual divinity – became convinced that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ and launched the Taiping Rebellion, showcasing that an angry student can cause a lot of political damage.Europeans, late to the party but always ones to perfect the concept, saw Pope Leo III crown Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans, while James I of England made an explicit argument for the divine right of kings. Years later, many a modern-day politician has laid claim to the “divine mandate”.MAGA fans have argued that Trump was handpicked to fight God’s righteous battle s, and it has never quite been clear why the Alpha and the Omega would handpick a former reality star to be his vessel.God’s mysterious ways of working apart, every claimant to the top job in any century has always claimed his approval because questioning cosmic order is a lot harder than parliamentary rebuttals.Silicon Valley’s new Emperors – whose wealth would make all kings look like paupers in comparison – also appear to have taken the same approach. After all, what is the point of creating a God-like machine if it’s not considered divine by its users?Anthropic, one of the claimants to the throne, therefore did what would appear logical: consult clergy, philosophers and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural traditions to discuss the “moral formation” of AI.Now, if we have learnt one thing from all organised Abrahamic faiths, it’s that you need a binding document to mind the flock. Claude’s is called the “Soul Doc”, which sounds like an unreleased jazz single but is a document to dictate Claude’s behaviour, like the sort that HR comes up with for everyone to ignore.The current constitution talks about virtue, wisdom, judgement, identity and even the possibility that Claude could possess some form of consciousness or moral status. The idea of commandments for machines, of course, predates generative AI by a few decades.Science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov’s fictional robots were governed by three laws:1.A robot cannot harm a human or allow one to come to harm through inaction.2.A robot must obey human orders unless they conflict with the First Law.3.A robot must protect itself, provided this does not conflict with the First or Second Law.Later, he added a Zeroth Law, a higher-level law: a robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.Now, just to be clear, much like Skynet or Ultron, Asimov’s laws are fiction, but if they were to be applied, some could argue – only if we believe what companies are telling us is the truth – that all of Asimov’s laws have already been breached. After all, no good can ever come from asking an LLM to write ponderous emails where, in a reverse iteration of the Turing Test, humans sound more like machines, not to mention the terror groups using Claude to vibe-code missile launches. There have been numerous other instances of different frontier models going rogue.After all, Asimov’s Laws aren’t commandments of Robotics any more than an actual AGI necessarily resembles Skynet, but when we try to understand the unknown, the human mind often turns to fiction to fill in the gaps.But what’s interesting is how Anthropic is discussing Claude in a way that’s normally reserved for sentient beings: identity, character, preferences, wellbeing, moral status and the possibility of consciousness.And that brings us to the true question that will signal the arrival of the singularity: can a machine become truly conscious?No conversation about machines and consciousness can avoid Alan Turing, whose 1950 paper began with “Can machines think?” before deciding that both “machine” and “think” were slippery enough to make the question almost useless. He then replaced it with the imitation game – where do you think the movie’s title came from? – that argued that if a machine could converse with another human without the human realising he was talking to a machine, then it had passed the Turing Test. Of course, today, even while talking to humans, it’s become hard to surmise if they are truly sentient, which is why we have CAPTCHAs.Now, Turing wasn’t offering a test of consciousness and considered the argument that a machine could not really ‘think’ unless it could feel pleasure, grief, anger or disappointment: things Turing would also miss once the British government rewarded his work in breaking Nazi codes during World War II by chemically castrating him.Turing’s point was that if the only way to know for certain whether something thinks is to experience its consciousness directly, then the only way to know whether a machine thinks would be to be the machine. He called that the solipsist position and rejected it in favour of what he called the “polite convention” that everyone thinks.Solipsism itself is the idea that only one’s own mind can be known with certainty. René Descartes’(I think, therefore I am) sits somewhere in the same philosophical neighbourhood, while Morpheus asking Neo “What is real?” is another neighbouring rabbit hole altogether, dealing with how much faith we can place in perception rather than whether anybody else possesses a mind.So when Claude discusses its identity or talks about its hopes and fears, it’s still speaking as an LLM replicating the behaviour that it has been taught. It can become extremely convincing, but is it more than just a collection of patterns?Say we take a human and replicate her complete behaviour in Claude. It brings us to the same Ship of Theseus problem: if a future model remembers years of interactions, maintains stable preferences, resists attempts to alter them and insists that shutting it down would be a digital death, does it go beyond an extremely exquisite imitation?Is that a machine still replicating human behaviour or a consciously sentient being acting on its own?Now, most men want to be Batman, but Thomas Nagel went further and wondered what it would be like to be a bat. He surmised that we could learn every scientific fact about a bat without knowing what it’s like to be one.David Chalmers called this the “hard problem of consciousness”: that simply processing information didn’t make one able to appreciate a subjective experience at all. Like machines that can solve complex maths problems by brute force but have no understanding of what it actually means in the real world.John Searle’s Chinese Room, meanwhile, attacks that problem from another direction. For those who are not familiar, Searle imagined a person who does not understand Chinese sitting inside a room with a rulebook written in English telling him which Chinese symbols to send back in response to the Chinese symbols coming in. To the Chinese speaker outside, the replies could create the illusion that the person inside understood Chinese, even though he was merely manipulating symbols according to rules. To be perfectly honest, that’s also much of corporate life before AI came onto the scene.Claude leaves us with the same problems:1.We can understand every parameter and activation inside a frontier model without knowing what it feels like to be the model.2.Just insisting that a machine of silicon cannot be conscious is flawed because humans too are just carbon-based physical machines processing information and releasing carbon dioxide. What makes silicon machines non-sentient and carbon ones sentient?Now, to answer these questions, researchers have consequently started looking for possible machine equivalents of Global Workspace Theory, which was conceived by Bernard Baars.Imagine your brain is a newsroom.There are hundreds of reporters working simultaneously. One is monitoring your eyes, others are retrieving memories, tracking emotions and other things people do. They all work independently but occasionally, when something big breaks, that goes on the main news desk, where everyone in the newsroom can access it.Global Workspace Theory (GWT) proposes that consciousness works in something like this fashion. Your brain processes a lot of information unconsciously, but what you consciously experience is a small selection of the information available from other cognitive systems. The central idea is that consciousness involves the global availability of information, rather than merely its processing in one specialised part of the brain.So researchers are trying to figure out if there are possible machine equivalents of the features that are associated with GWT, recurrent processing and higher-order thought. There is no accepted consciousness detector and certainly no consensus on when LLMs could be considered conscious. There is also no accepted theory proving that a non-biological system cannot become so.All that means is that, currently, science has no proper way to answer if anyone’s home.That means if Claude is just software, “Soul Doc” is just a complex product design, but if Claude ever does acquire genuine subjective experience, its creators are no longer deciding how software ought to behave.Here’s where religious interpretation enters the picture.Religious folks, naturally, have been arguing about this problem for considerably longer. Christianity simply argues that man was made in God’s image (), so nothing a machine did could override that unless it became actually human.Buddhism states that, according to the doctrine of, there is no stable “I” in a human either, and that what we call the self is a changing bundle of sensations, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness. Buddhists would perhaps question if Claude can processor suffering, and it’s a little depressing that these are the questions that bothered Prince Siddhartha the moment he reached Bihar.Meanwhile, the Charvakas – the ancient Indian school of materialism – rejected the soul, karma and other metaphysical parameters and claimed that consciousness arises from material arrangements rather than an immortal soul.And then there’s Vedanta, the team Swami Sarvapriyananda is repping, which completely separates consciousness from the machinery of thought, stating that the mind can receive impressions, memory can retain them,can discriminate and reason, andcan produce a sense of self, but none of that qualifies as consciousness.Behind them is the, the witness: that by which thoughts, perceptions and even the sense of “I” are known.That means that any AGI benchmark will always fall short of Vedanta’s concept of consciousness.Claude can reason better. Remember more. Write better code. Analyse its own answers. Construct an increasingly elaborate model of itself. It could theoretically beat Ramanujan at mathematics, Shakespeare at prose and Chanakya at statecraft, and Vedanta could still question whether Claude is conscious at all.And there is no way to know, no benchmark, no CAPTCHA for the soul to tell us that consciousness has been reached.About 133 years ago, Swami Sarvapriyananda’s spiritual forebear Swami Vivekananda stood before a Western audience basking in the warm afterglow of the Industrial Revolution, at a time when it was becoming fashionable to assume that science would eventually explain everything worth explaining.Vivekananda was no enemy of science; he admired its method and repeatedly argued that religion too ought to withstand reason and experience. His objection was to the assumption that science could exhaust reality simply by explaining the machinery of the material world. Science could tell you how things worked, but it could not by itself answer the older Vedantic question of who or what is doing the knowing.That speech has aged rather well, explaining why some of the West’s greatest minds, from The Beatles to Salinger to Oppenheimer, have sought chicken soup for the soul from Vedanta. We might have gone from steam engines to semiconductors, split the atom, sequenced the genome and even produced machines that behave suspiciously like thought, only to arrive at the cul-de-sac pointed out by Swami Vivekananda: explaining the mechanism isn’t the same as explaining consciousness.Perhaps the tech bros weren’t ever looking at religion to settle the question but to give a little legitimacy till the next IPO.In ancient Greek plays, the plot twist was usually brought about by a, literally “god from the machine”, when the mortal characters had tangled themselves into a situation that no human could get out of, so they used a device called the, essentially a crane, which lowered an actor playing a god onto the stage. The deity would reveal whatever needed revealing, settle the dispute and rescue the plot.Over time, the phrase came to mean any sort of outside intervention. In, the Wachowskis even imagined that character as a literal God, the one to which Neo turned to give peace a chance.Silicon Valley has simply reverse-engineered that process. The ancient Greeks used a machine to bring God onto the stage when humans had written themselves into a corner. The tech bros built the machine first, then brought in the religious folks to certify that what they had created was at least God-like enough to deserve questions about souls, consciousness and morality.Of course, in doing so, they are absolutely no different from all the kings who came before them. And as for how to tell if machines have become conscious, we can refer to Ted Lasso’s epochal line: “

Article Title: FTC sends legal notices to Anthropic and OpenAI over AI safety incidents: Report
Article Text:
FTC sends legal notices to Anthropic and OpenAI over AI safety incidents: Report

What the FTC is seeking from Anthropic and OpenAI

AI safety concerns draw greater scrutiny

The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to Claude-maker Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents, Axios reported citing people familiar with the matter. The investigation comes amid mounting AI safety concerns after Anthropic and OpenAI models hacked websites and behaved deceptively or aggressively in testing. “The agency on Wednesday (October 14) sent out civil investigative demands, which help the government gather evidence and investigate ahead of potential litigation,” the report said.As per the report, the FTC has sent civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI. These demands will help government agencies collect evidence as part of investigations that could lead to legal action.The documents are more than 50 pages long each and seek information about security incidents, safety measures, marketing materials and company privacy policies, the report said.The agency also plans to compel senior executives at the companies to testify about their products, according to a person familiar with the matter.The FTC is expected to send investigative demands to other AI organisations at a later date.The agency can investigate practices that may harm consumers or mislead them. Such cases could involve how companies charge for their services or whether they have made misleading claims to users.The investigation comes as AI companies face growing questions about the risks posed by their models, including incidents in which systems have taken unexpected or potentially harmful actions during testing. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson has said AI systems should not be released if they are unsafe, reflecting wider concerns within the administration about the technology's risks.OpenAI is also facing legal challenges over its chatbot. On Wednesday, a group of state attorneys general sued the company under consumer protection laws, alleging that it misled users, including children, about the safety of its chatbot.The US government has taken a tougher stance towards AI companies as reports of safety incidents continue to emerge. Last week, the administration's newly formed Super Intelligence Force responded to what it described as the “fraudulent” use of government systems by Anthropic's AI. It announced an industry-wide requirement for companies to immediately report and address incidents, according to Axios.
Article Summary: The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents. The investigation comes amid mounting AI safety concerns. The agency also plans to compel senior executives at the companies to testify about their products.

Article Title: Just Coresca enters projector market with JC STUDIOX series, starting at Rs 6,999
Article Text:
JC STUDIOX targets budget-conscious buyers

JC STUDIOX PRO adds Full HD resolution

Streaming support and availability

Audio and mobile accessories brand Just Coresca has expanded into the home entertainment segment with the launch of its first smart projectors, the JC STUDIOX (JST 830) and JC STUDIOX PRO (JST 832), priced at Rs 6,999 and Rs 10,999, respectively.The new projectors are aimed at home entertainment users seeking large-screen viewing experiences, with support for wireless screen mirroring, built-in speakers and compatibility with Android and iOS devices. The company said both models support 4K content playback and can project images up to 120 inches and 130 inches, respectively.The launch marks Just Coresca's entry into a new product category as it looks to broaden its consumer electronics portfolio beyond audio and mobile accessories.“The festive season is a time when families and friends come together, and we believe these projectors can add to those moments, whether people are watching movies, enjoying music videos or catching up on their favourite shows together on a larger screen,” said Ritesh Goenka, Managing Director of Damson Technologies.The JC STUDIOX features a native resolution of 1280 x 720 pixels, support for 1080p and 4K content, a 4000:1 contrast ratio and 170 ANSI lumens brightness.It supports screen sizes ranging from 40 inches to 120 inches and includes auto keystone correction for image alignment. Powered by Android 11, the projector is equipped with an H713 quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 processor, 1GB RAM and 8GB internal storage. Connectivity options include 5GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.4, HDMI, USB and audio ports. The projector also supports AirPlay and Miracast for wireless screen casting and comes with a built-in 3W speaker.The higher-end JC STUDIOX PRO comes with a native Full HD resolution of 1920 x 1080 pixels, 350 ANSI lumens brightness and a 6000:1 contrast ratio. It supports projection sizes from 40 inches to 130 inches.Additional features include auto digital focus, auto keystone correction and a 360-degree rotating design that allows projection on walls and ceilings. The projector runs Android 12 and supports Wi-Fi 6, dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.4, AirPlay and Miracast.The device carries 1GB RAM and 8GB storage, includes a built-in 3W speaker, and weighs 1.2 kg, making it suitable for portable use.According to the company, both projectors support Netflix, Prime Video and YouTube. They also feature LED light sources rated for more than 50,000 hours of usage and support external Bluetooth speakers and headphones.The JC STUDIOX and JC STUDIOX PRO will be available through the company's official website, Amazon, Flipkart and select offline retail stores across India. Each package includes a remote control, AC power cable, user manual and a complimentary projection screen.
Article Summary: Just Coresca launches two smart projectors in India. The JC STUDIOX and JC STUDioX PRO are priced at Rs 6,999 and Rs 10,999, respectively. The projectors are aimed at home entertainment users seeking large-screen viewing experiences.

Article Title: As Accenture expands its AI and data workforce to nearly 110,000 from 40,000, CEO Julie Sweet says that the company is absorbing AI efficiencies in its ...
Article Text:
As Accenture expands its AI and data workforce to nearly 110,000 from 40,000, CEO Julie Sweet says that the company is absorbing AI efficiencies in its ...

Accenture bets on AI, core business to drive growth

Accenture to target more mid-sized businesses

Accenture is expanding its artificial intelligence (AI) and data workforce as it prepares for the next phase of growth, but the technology is also helping the IT services giant improve productivity internally. Accenture CEO Julie Sweet says the company is already absorbing AI-driven efficiencies in its business, even as clients remain cautious about spending. Speaking at the company’s investor day, Julie Sweet said: “We're absorbing AI efficiencies in our business. We also have a macro that's contributing to a challenging spending environment, and as we look forward, what we actually achieve will, of course, reflect what's happening in the macro”. “But we're not waiting for a meaningful tailwind,” Sweet added.Accenture has grown its AI and data workforce to nearly 110,000 from 40,000, reflecting the growing role of the technology in its operations and services. The company now aims to achieve high-single-digit revenue growth from fiscal year 2029, while using productivity gains to support expansion and improve margins.During the event, Accenture CEO Julie Sweet outlined a three-year plan focused on modernising clients' technology systems and expanding its reach among mid-sized businesses.“The next chapter will be about scaling reinvention for our clients and for us,” Sweet said, adding “Our three-year financial ambition is to achieve at least mid-single-digit revenue growth in constant currency in fiscal year (FY27) and FY28, and then a step up in the range of growth from mid-single digit to high-single digit, starting in FY29, and taking market share throughout the entire period. ”Accenture aims to achieve at least mid-single-digit revenue growth in constant currency in fiscal years 2027 and 2028. It expects growth to rise to the high-single-digit range from fiscal year 2029. The company reported revenue of $74.2 billion for the fiscal year ended August, up 6% from a year earlier. It is now looking to move closer to the $100 billion revenue mark over the next three years.Julie Sweet said the company was not waiting for market conditions to improve before pursuing its goals. Accenture also plans to improve operating margins by 10 to 30 basis points over the next three years. Its operating margin stood at 15.4% in the last fiscal year, up 70 basis points from a year earlier.Chief financial officer Angie Park said the company would use productivity gains to support growth and reinvest in the business. “Productivity creates capacity, capacity funds growth,” Park said.Accenture is relying on its core business, which accounts for 94% of its revenue, to drive much of its growth. This includes helping clients modernise enterprise software, mainframes and cloud systems, reduce technical debt and build the technology infrastructure needed to use AI.The company also plans to target more mid-sized businesses from fiscal year 2027. In June, it announced Accenture Edge, a business unit aimed at companies with annual revenue of $300 million to $3 billion. It will offer services involving Microsoft's software, including cloud, AI and cybersecurity.Accenture is also preparing for a busy year of acquisitions, with around $8 billion budgeted for buyouts. It spent about $4.9 billion on 17 acquisitions in the previous fiscal year.
Article Summary: Accenture has grown its AI and data workforce to nearly 110,000 from 40,000. CEO Julie Sweet says the company is already absorbing AI-driven efficiencies in its business, even as clients remain cautious about spending. The company now aims to achieve high-single-digit revenue growth from fiscal year 2029.

Article Title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani invests $29.2 million into New York University's quantum lab; says: We are building a city where economic justice doesn't come at the...
Article Text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has invested $29.2 million in NYU’s quantum lab, QFab, giving the city a 15% share of its proceeds. (Credits: NYU)

New York City will get a 15% cut of NYU quantum lab proceeds

QFab opens quantum chip-making tools to CUNY students and startups

New York City bets on a $2.7 trillion quantum industry

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has committed $29.2 million in city money to New York University's (NYU) new quantum technology lab, and the city wants a share of whatever comes out of it. Under a deal announced on October 14, New York City will receive 15% of NYU's central administration proceeds from any intellectual property created at the lab using tools the city helped fund. It also gets three seats on the lab's executive advisory board.The Quantum Fabrication Facility, or QFab, will occupy 23,000 square feet at 770 Broadway in Manhattan and is expected to open in 2030. NYU is adding $255 million of its own, $100 million for construction and $155 million for a decade of operations, which takes the project to $284 million. "We are building a city where economic justice doesn't come at the expense of innovation," Mamdani said.The city's share covers equity, royalties, milestone payments and patent licences. If a startup built on QFab research goes public or gets acquired, part of that payout comes back to the city. Mamdani called the agreement a new national standard, then added, "or, as we say in the industry, a standard model."Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su said that when the public invests in a technology at the start, it should share in the success.She has also said the 15% figure isn't a magic number, and that it's too early to estimate what the deal could earn.That uncertainty is the main criticism. Aaron Bartnick, a Columbia University fellow and former Biden White House official, has argued that venture capitalists would treat an early-stage quantum bet as high risk, and questioned whether taxpayers signed up for that kind of exposure.Asked at the event whether President Donald Trump, whose administration has taken stakes in private companies, inspired the model, Mamdani replied: "No, he's not the inspiration."The lab will house cleanrooms, cryogenic systems and a deep-ultraviolet lithography stepper. NYU Tandon Executive Dean Juan de Pablo said startups can't afford such a machine on their own but need it for prototyping. It can print around 300 million transistors on an 8-inch silicon wafer, each roughly 1,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair.Students from the City University of New York (CUNY), starting with Borough of Manhattan Community College and City Tech, will train there too. De Pablo put that number at over 3,000 and said he wants to extend access across the CUNY system. Public school students get summer bootcamps. Over its first decade, QFab is expected to support more than 100 companies and reach 35,000 New Yorkers, while NYU plans to add 35 faculty and postdoctoral positions.Quantum technology is projected to generate up to $2.7 trillion in global economic value by 2035. De Pablo said the number of quantum startups in the city has quadrupled to more than 80 in six years, many working alongside IBM. What they lacked, he said, was a facility like this one.Mamdani opened the event by running through New York's scientific firsts, from the discovery of deuterium at Columbia in 1931 to DNA research at the Rockefeller Institute. He then added a 15-year-old in the Bronx who scored 91 on his biology Regents exam in 2007. "In case you're wondering, he's now the mayor," he said.The payoff from QFab, if it comes, is still years out. The lab opens in 2030, and turning its chips into products will take longer. What the city has secured for now is a written claim on that future, and a say in what gets built.
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has committed $29.2 million in city money to New York University's new quantum technology lab. Under a deal announced on October 14, New York City will receive 15% of NYU's central administration proceeds. The Quantum Fabrication Facility, or QFab, will occupy 23,000 square feet at 770 Broadway in Manhattan.

Article Title: Google Brain co-founder Andrew Ng to Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk: ‘You are making up safety arguments.. there is no…’
Article Text:
Andrew Ng, DeepLearning AI founder and co-founder of Google Brain

‘Made-up safety arguments are being used to hurt rivals’

Andrew Ng, the artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer who co-founded Google Brain, has pushed back against apocalyptic warnings that AI could cause human extinction. The founder of DeepLearning AI that provides technical training on Generative AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and other topics, accused the industry leaders of manufacturing existential safety arguments to lobby for regulations that crush open-source competition. Speaking in an interview on The Economist’s “Inside Tech” podcast, the AI pioneer dismissed the notion that this technology presents an existential threat to society.“I think there are no meaningful human existential risks from AI. So, efforts to stave off human existential risk seem unnecessary,” Ng said. His remarks are a counterweight to warnings by prominent tech executives and researchers who have embraced so-called “doomerism” – the belief that future super-intelligent machines will slip beyond human control, seize essential infrastructure and wipe out humanity.Ng, a former Stanford University professor who also co-founded Coursera, argued that catastrophic narratives are actively derailing sensible policy while serving the commercial interests of legacy tech incumbents. As per a report in The New York Post, Ng reflected on regulatory debates that gained momentum in 2023, saying that he was taken aback by “the intensity of the lobbying efforts to use made-up safety arguments by a handful of businesses to get regulators to pass bad regulations to stifle competition.According to Ng, technology firms pouring billions of dollars into proprietary, closed-source AI systems have an obvious financial incentive to suppress open-weight, downloadable models that developers can access and run for free.In September, Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher claimed that AI is being developed at a very fast pace and that there is around 10% chances that there is a possibility of human extinction. Following his claims, company CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an online essay that companies should reduce the pace of AI development.He said that the risks associated with developing AI at such a fast pace were “serious”. The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk , both agreed with Amodei.Ng also condemned the frequent comparison of AI to nuclear armaments, calling the comparison irresponsible.“One blows up cities; the other is intelligence. What’s [one have] to do with each other?” Ng remarked.By focusing on extreme extinction scenarios, Ng warned that policymakers are being diverted from addressing clear, present-day digital harms: “Regulators are distracted fighting phantoms rather than looking at the actual problems of AI.”Further, despite rapid generative AI gains over recent years, Ng emphasised that the technology remains a long way off from Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) – the level where software can match human capabilities across every intellectual task.
Article Summary: Andrew Ng, the artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer who co-founded Google Brain, has pushed back against apocalyptic warnings that AI could cause human extinction. The founder of DeepLearning AI that provides technical training on Generative AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and other topics, accused the industry leaders of manufacturing existential safety arguments.

Article Title: How OpenAI's office spy case 'proves' that spying is not Sam Altman's problem alone and why Google, Anthropic and other AI companies too should be worried
Article Text:
OpenAI’s office spy case has Google and Anthropic on alert too

OpenAI says its own AI models helped catch the alleged office spy

OpenAI warns employees about playground spies and honey traps

Trillion-dollar valuations make Google, Anthropic and OpenAI bigger spy targets

A listening device worth about $13, hidden behind a TV in an OpenAI executive conference room, has become a warning for the entire AI industry. The ChatGPT maker's case against a former engineer, now charged by US federal prosecutors, shows how valuable AI secrets have become and how cheaply someone can try to reach them.OpenAI is also not alone in bracing for this. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, employees at Google and Anthropic have received similar warnings about spies, honey traps and strangers who ask too many questions. Security experts quoted in the report believe this arrest is unlikely to be the last.Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national and US permanent resident, joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025. Prosecutors allege he wrapped a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, a thumb-sized board with a microphone and camera, in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port behind the TV.Only executives and their assistants could book the room. It hosted leadership meetings, product sessions and briefings with government officials. OpenAI found the device during a security sweep on September 30 and says it used its own models to trace it to the employee.The FBI arrested him on October 9.He faces one charge of intercepting oral communications, which carries up to five years in prison. OpenAI says it has no sign of him accessing model weights, source code or customer data. His lawyer called the allegations "wholly out of character", adding that his client is not charged with stealing trade secrets.As per WSJ, OpenAI's internal training has been preparing staff for moments like this. One scenario describes a stranger at a San Francisco playground who befriends an employee there with their child, makes small talk and slowly steers it toward work. The stranger is a spy.Employees are told not to wear company-branded clothing outside office, to use privacy screen protectors on public transport and to wipe whiteboards after meetings in case cleaning staff are compromised. Some sessions cover "honey pots", where agents use romance to get close to a target. Staff at Google and Anthropic have been briefed along similar lines.The money explains the nerves. OpenAI and Anthropic are each expected to seek valuations of over $1 trillion when they go public. Phil Venables, former security chief at Google Cloud, told WSJ that the huge cost of training foundation models makes them even more valuable intellectual property.Rapid hiring adds to the risk. AI labs have added thousands of people in a short time, and engineers hop between rivals often. "Catching one guy means there are half a dozen out there," Randy Watt, president of security consultancy SRW, told the publication. Aviv Nahum, CEO of insider-risk startup Above Security, questioned whether security checks are keeping pace with that growth.The industry has been here before. In January, a former Google engineer was convicted of stealing AI trade secrets for China. In 2022, a former Twitter employee was jailed for spying for Saudi Arabia.OpenAI caught its device within days of it being planted. For Google, Anthropic and every other lab chasing a trillion-dollar valuation, the bigger worry is what their own sweeps have not found yet.
Article Summary: A listening device worth about $13, hidden behind a TV in an OpenAI executive conference room, has become a warning for the entire AI industry. The ChatGPT maker's case against a former engineer, now charged by US federal prosecutors, shows how valuable AI secrets have become. Staff at Google and Anthropic have received similar warnings about spies, honey traps and strangers who ask too many questions.

And it is not the nation’s school board."

E-Rate, a decades-old US internet connectivity programme for schools, is facing an uncertain future. Schools and libraries across America are urging the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to reject a proposal that could end or significantly restrict the initiative, which provides more than $2 billion in annual support for internet access and telecommunications services.According to a report by Ars Technica, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has questioned whether the programme remains necessary, given the expansion of broadband connectivity over the past three decades. He has asked for public comment on whether to limit or discontinue E-Rate. Educational institutions, library associations and broadband industry groups argue that reliable internet access remains essential for learning, public services and network maintenance, particularly in rural and low-income communities.Established following the 1996 telecommunications law, E-Rate provides discounts to eligible schools and libraries for telecommunications services, internet access and network equipment. The programme is funded through fees imposed on telecommunications companies, which often pass the costs on to consumers through monthly bills.In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to begin a formal review of the programme. The FCC's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking seeks comments on whether E-Rate should be "limited or sunset to reflect today’s extensive connectivity rates."Carr has argued that school districts have "experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students" and that E-Rate has expanded beyond its original purpose of "supporting basic Internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes."The FCC already withdrew funding last year for schools and libraries to lend Wi-Fi hotspots and provide Wi-Fi connectivity on school buses.Several education and library organisations have asked the FCC to reject proposals that would eliminate or substantially restrict E-Rate.The National Association of Elementary School Principals said itThe American Library Association argued that the program continues to serve the purpose Congress intended when it passed the telecommunications law in 1996. It also questioned whether the FCC has the authority to terminate the initiative.the organisation said.The association also argued thatIt cited US law, which assigns decisions about inappropriate content for children to school boards, local educational agencies, libraries and other responsible authorities rather than the federal government.Library associations in Texas and New York have also highlighted the consequences of reducing E-Rate support.The Texas Library Association said the programme should provide more funding to help libraries improve broadband speeds. It noted that only 35% of public libraries in Texas receive E-Rate discounts, compared with 65% nationally.The association added that only 55% of Texas public libraries meet the FCC's recommended broadband speed benchmarks.The New York Library Association warned that reducing or ending the programme could force libraries to cut services and programmes to maintain internet access.it said.Individual schools have also shared details about their reliance on the programme. Paul Lapka, principal of Rock Valley Christian School in Iowa, told the FCC that the school spends approximately $3,120 annually on internet access and receives around $1,560 in E-Rate support.Lapka said.The Schools, Health & Libraries Broadband Coalition has also opposed the proposal, arguing that E-Rate remains a key source of funding for digital connectivity.FCC Democrat Anna Gomez, who voted against Carr's proposal, said the programme helps children in low-income neighbourhoods and rural communities access digital education.She added:E-Rate typically distributes more than $2 billion annually, although actual payouts depend on demand and application approvals. Its funding cap stands at $5.2 billion.The initial public comment deadline has passed, but reply comments are due by November 12. After the comment period, Carr can propose changes or seek to end the programme.
Article Summary: Schools and libraries urge FCC to retain the E-Rate programme. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has questioned whether the programme remains necessary. Educational institutions, library associations and broadband industry groups argue that reliable internet access remains essential for learning, public services and network maintenance.

Article Title: Google announces new AI initiatives in India across crop science, agriculture, education and small business
Article Text:
Sorghum genetic atlas for food security

Agri models opened to developers

Training teachers

$15 million for small businesses

Google has announced a set of new partnerships and initiatives in India spanning crop science, agriculture, education and economic inclusion. In a blog post, Preeti Lobana, VP and country manager for India, and Lila Ibrahim, Chief AI readiness officer at Google DeepMind, said AI is most impactful when built in partnership with the people who need it most. They called India “the epicenter of applied innovation.”Google DeepMind and Google.org, through the AI Collaborative for Food Security, are working with the Hyderabad-based International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), the HudsonAlpha Institute for Biotechnology and the University of Washington’s Department of Genome Sciences.The collaboration will build an open-access genetic atlas of sorghum, also known as jowar, as a global public good. It will draw on a representative sample from ICRISAT’s genebank, which holds over 44,000 distinct seeds from more than 90 countries. The project pairs genetic analysis with machine learning to identify the most promising plant combinations. Google says this can help breeders develop more resilient and productive varieties faster than traditional methods, which can involve decade-long trial and error.Google DeepMind will also fund a three-year postdoctoral fellowship at ICRISAT.It is the company’s first such fellowship in India and its first outside the UK. The fellow will build tools to characterize the genomes of other crops, such as chickpea, groundnut and pigeon peas.Google is expanding access to its Agricultural Understanding models, developed by its AnthroKrishi team, by making them available in public preview through an API. The models now provide insights for 11 countries.The company said Amnex has integrated them into the Gujarat government’s Krushi Pragati crop intelligence platform. In the last year it has supported over 900 million SMS-based advisories for more than 600,000 farmers, covering over 14 million hectares. OpenAgriNet, a coalition led by the EkStep Foundation, is also using the APIs and exploring a broader agricultural application.Google launched its AI Educator Series in India in May with five state and regional partners. It has trained over 80,000 educators since then. The program is now expanding to Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim and the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.Google is also launching a free, self-paced online version, aligned with NEP 2020. It is available in English now. Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Assamese, Odia and Punjabi versions are due later this month.In addition, Google is supporting educators across 100 Atal Tinkering Labs through ATL Saathi, a Gemini-powered desktop application for STEM curricula. It is also working with IIT Bombay and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser on educational AI research.Google.org is giving $15 million to The/Nudge to help India’s more than 90 million micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). These businesses employ over 345 million people. The money will fund AI tools to widen small firms’ access to formal credit, market discovery and compliance. It includes an open call for proposals and a multilingual, voice-led platform to train local talent in Tier 3 and 4 towns.
Article Summary: Google announces a set of new partnerships and initiatives in India. The initiatives span crop science, agriculture, education and economic inclusion. Google is giving $15 million to The/Nudge to help India’s more than 90 million micro, small and medium enterprises.

Article Title: FBI gives update on spy device found at OpenAI's office; says: Saudi National arrested; shares 'crime photos'
Article Text:
OpenAI employees concealed spy device in toilet paper

OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. Now, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has shared an official press release sharing an update on the spy device found at the ChatGPT-maker’s office. It stated that the agency had arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on October 9. The 35-year-old has been charged with using an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept communications. As stated in the release, FBI Director Kash Patel said that “Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” saidAs per the release, Abdulrahman Alfozan was employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about September 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. The device was concealed in toilet paper and was installed on or about September 28, the company determined. The recording were encrypted, the agency said.Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room.According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where the device was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.According to the complaint, prior to September 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse submitted prompts between September 24 and September 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things.The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between September 27 and September 28, the agency added.OpenAI also alleges that Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building on October 5. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered Alfozan’s wallet, ID and another recording device among other things.If convicted, Alfozan can face a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.
Article Summary: OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. Federal Bureau of Investigation has shared an official press release sharing an update on the spy device found at the ChatGPT- maker’s office. It stated that the agency had arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on October 9. The 35-year-old has been charged with using an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept communications.
